questions.question: Non-negative integrable gains X,Y have equal means and Y second-order dominates X. Must every increasing concave utility strictly prefer Y, including the linear utility $u(w)=w$?
options: No; the linear utility is indifferent because the means agree.
Yes; second-order dominance requires strict preference for every utility.
Yes; linear utility becomes strictly concave when gains are random.
No; linear increasing utility is excluded from the comparison class.

questions.question: A proposed second-order comparison of non-negative gains checks $\int_0^{10}F_X(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\ge\int_0^{10}F_Y(s)\,\mathrm{d}s$. What additional range of checks is required to conclude Y dominates X?
options: Only the CDF values at threshold ten.
The same direction at every non-negative threshold.
Only the two probabilities at zero.
Only the mean comparison once this one area check passes.

questions.question: Non-negative integrable gains X,Y have equal integrated CDF areas at every threshold $t\ge 0$. What does this imply about their distributions?
options: They must be independent because both weak dominance directions hold.
They have equal means but can have different distributions.
They have the same distribution, though they need not be the same random outcome.
Their CDFs may differ at a jump while all integrated areas remain equal.

questions.question: A non-negative gain W is zero with probability 0.2 and three with probability 0.8. What is its integrated CDF area $\int_0^2F_W(s)\,\mathrm{d}s$?
An integrable gain X has mean one and a proposed dominant gain Y has mean 0.8. What does the necessary mean condition say about Y second-order dominating X?
options: It follows because Y may have a smaller variance.
Y fails the necessary mean bound, since0.8 is below one.
It follows because both means are positive.
It cannot be assessed until the two means are equal.

questions.question: Non-negative gains X,Y satisfy second-order dominance of Y over X. Both are converted to amounts $X^*=2X+3$, $Y^*=2Y+3$. Why does the same dominance direction hold for the converted amounts?
options: Doubling outcomes reverses all integrated CDF inequalities.
Adding three makes all random gains certain.
A positive scale and common cash shift preserve utility preferences.
The two converted gains must have equal means.

questions.question: Non-negative integrable gains X,Y have equal means, and Y second-order dominates X. Which convex-order relation is guaranteed for every pair satisfying these premises?
options: $Y\le_{\mathrm{cx}}X$.
$X\le_{\mathrm{cx}}Y$.
$Y\le_{\mathrm{cx}}X$ only when their laws are equal.
Neither convex-order direction is available even with equal means.

questions.question: Gain Y is certainly one and X is zero or two with equal probability, so Y second-order dominates X. An analyst applies the increasing transformation $h(w)=w^2$ to both gains and claims the same dominance direction must remain. Which test rejects that claim?
options: No; transformed means differ, and second-order dominance requires equal means.
Yes; increasing transformations preserve the increasing-concave utility comparisons.
Yes; the transformed certain gain has smaller variance, which suffices for dominance.
No; linear utility prefers the transformed random gain with mean two over the certain gain one.

questions.question: For non-negative integrable gains X,Y,Z, Y second-order dominates X and Z second-order dominates Y; utility expectations are defined. Which comparison is guaranteed for every triple satisfying these premises?
options: X second-order dominates Z.
X and Z must have identical laws.
No gain comparison follows unless all three means are equal.
Z second-order dominates X.

questions.question: Gain X is one or five with equal probabilities, and Y is two or four with equal probabilities. Let $D(t)=\int_0^t(F_X(s)-F_Y(s))\,\mathrm{d}s$. It is zero up to one, rises to 0.5 by two, stays 0.5 through four, and decreases to zero by five, remaining zero afterwards. Which whole-range conclusion follows?
options: X second-order dominates Y because X has the larger maximum.
Neither dominates because the CDFs cross between their support points.
Y second-order dominates X despite their crossing CDFs.
Their laws are identical because both integrated areas agree beyond five.

questions.question: Initial wealth is six. Loss X is certainly two, while loss Y is zero or four with equal probabilities. Which final-wealth second-order comparison expresses the risk-averse preference?
options: Certain wealth four dominates the equally likely wealths two and six.
The equally likely wealths two and six dominate certain wealth four.
Certain wealth two dominates the equally likely wealths zero and four.
The two wealth laws are equal because the two loss means agree.

questions.question: Gain X is certainly one; gain Y is zero with probability 0.2 and three with probability 0.8. Compare them using increasing concave utilities $u(w)=\log(1+w)$ and $v(w)=\min(w,1)$ on non-negative gains. What do the two expected-utility rankings establish?
options: Y dominates X because one increasing concave utility prefers Y.
Neither gain second-order dominates the other.
X dominates Y because the capped increasing concave utility prefers X.
The two rankings are inadmissible because utility must be linear.

questions.question: Gain X is certainly one and gain Y certainly four, so Y dominates X in both first and second order. A purported utility witness $u(w)=w-w^2/4$ gives $u(Y)=0<u(X)=3/4$. Why does this not refute second-order dominance?
options: Second-order dominance allows only equal-mean gain comparisons.
The quadratic is increasing but convex on the gain range.
Expected utility must instead be evaluated at expected gain before applying u.
The quadratic is concave but fails to be increasing on the gain range.

questions.question: Equal-mean gains X,Y both have mean two. X is one or three with equal probability. Y is zero with probability 1/10 and 20/9 with probability 9/10; their variances are one and 4/9. Does the lower variance establish Y second-order dominating X? At threshold 1/2, test $I_X(t)\ge I_Y(t)$.
options: No; the areas are $0<1/20$, so the required direction fails.
Yes; equal means and lower variance are sufficient for dominance.
Yes; Y has the smaller maximum gain and therefore less risk.
No; the means are unequal because Y has a zero outcome.

questions.question: Gain X is zero or four with equal probabilities. Gain Y is one with probability p and five with probability $1-p$, where $0\le p\le 1$. For exactly which p does Y second-order dominate X? Check the full integrated-CDF comparison, not only the mean.
options: Every $p\in[0,1]$.
